topics.title: Arthur C. Clarke and life on a space station

learn.hook: Can a tiny bird be useful hundreds of kilometres above the Earth? A famous science fiction writer thought so!
points: 'Feathered Friend' is a science fiction story by Arthur C. Clarke in which a small pet bird on a space station turns out to matter far more than anyone expected.

Arthur C. Clarke (1917-2008) was a British writer of science fiction who lived in Sri Lanka from 1956 until his death. In 1945 he wrote about using satellites in space to send signals around the world.
In the past, miners took canaries into coal mines. These birds react to dangerous gases like carbon monoxide sooner than people do, so a canary in trouble warned miners to get out.
On a space station, astronauts float because they are in free fall around the Earth (often called weightlessness or microgravity). Air, water and food must be carried up or recycled.
The International Space Station orbits about 400 km above the Earth and goes around it roughly every 90 minutes.

example.q: Read this original passage: 'On Moon Base Chandra, Ravi grew tomatoes under bright lamps. One morning every plant was drooping, though he had watered them the night before. He checked the water recycler and found it had stopped working.' Think it through: how did the plants help Ravi?
steps: Ravi had watered the plants, so drooping was unexpected.
The drooping was a warning sign that something was wrong.
Ravi checked the water recycler and found the fault.
So the plants acted like an early warning system.
example.answer: The drooping plants warned Ravi that the water recycler had failed, so he could find and fix the problem.

learn.reallife: Many homes today have smoke detectors and gas alarms that do the job miners' canaries once did: they warn us early about danger.

games.title: Space and Clarke facts
items: Arthur C. Clarke lived in Sri Lanka for many years.
He lived there from 1956 until his death in 2008.
Canaries were used in coal mines to warn of dangerous gases.
The birds showed signs of trouble before people did.
Astronauts on a space station float because there is no Earth gravity at all up there.
Gravity still acts on them. They float because they and the station are in free fall around the Earth.
The International Space Station orbits about 400 km above the Earth.
It goes around the Earth roughly every 90 minutes.
On a space station, fresh air can be got simply by opening a window.
Space has no air to breathe. Air must be carried, made or recycled inside.
Arthur C. Clarke wrote mainly about magic and fairies.
He wrote science fiction, based on science and technology.

revise.summary: 'Feathered Friend' is a science fiction story by Arthur C. Clarke in which a small pet bird on a space station turns out to matter far more than anyone expected. The lesson also explains how canaries once warned coal miners of dangerous gases.
focus: Recall facts about Arthur C. Clarke (1917-2008), who lived in Sri Lanka from 1956.
Explain why miners took canaries into coal mines.
Know basic facts about life on a space station.

topics.title: Science fiction: imagining tomorrow with science

learn.hook: A robot that cooks dosa, a bus to Mars, a phone that translates birdsong. If it uses science to imagine the future, it's science fiction!
points: Science fiction (sci-fi) is imaginative writing based on science and technology. It asks 'What if...?' about the future, space, inventions or other worlds.
Sci-fi is different from fantasy: fantasy uses magic, while sci-fi tries to explain things through science, even when the science is imagined.
Common features: future or space settings, new inventions, scientists or astronauts as characters, and problems solved by reasoning.
Some sci-fi ideas later came true, such as communication satellites, video calls and robots.

India has its own sci-fi tradition, including Satyajit Ray's stories about the inventor Professor Shonku. India's real space journey includes Rakesh Sharma, the first Indian in space (1984), and Chandrayaan-3, which landed near the Moon's south pole on 23 August 2023.

example.q: Think it through: Is this science fiction or fantasy? 'In 2090, Asha boarded a solar-powered shuttle to a farm on Mars, where robots grew wheat inside glass domes.'
steps: Look at the setting: the future (2090) and Mars.
Look at the technology: a solar-powered shuttle, robots, glass domes.
Is there any magic? No, everything is explained by technology.
So it is science fiction.

learn.reallife: Space missions by ISRO, like Chandrayaan and the Gaganyaan human spaceflight programme, show how yesterday's sci-fi dreams become today's science.

steps: Sci-fi explains events with real or imagined science.
Fantasy explains them with magic.

learn.hook: An 'astronaut' is a star sailor! Many science words hide old Greek and Latin roots. Crack the code and you can guess new words!
points: Many science words are built from roots and prefixes that come from Greek or Latin.
tele = far (telephone, telescope, television); micro = very small (microscope, microphone); astro/astr = star (astronaut, astronomy).
bio = life (biology, biography); geo = earth (geography, geology); photo = light (photograph, photosynthesis); hydro = water (hydropower).
scope = look at (telescope, microscope); graph = write or draw (autograph, photograph); phone = sound (telephone, microphone); naut = sailor (astronaut).
logy = study of (biology, geology, zoology). So geology is the study of the earth.

example.q: Think it through: Use roots to work out what a 'microscope' does and what 'biology' means.
steps: micro = very small; scope = look at. A microscope helps you look at very small things.
bio = life; logy = study of. Biology is the study of living things.
example.answer: A microscope is for looking at very small things; biology is the study of life.

learn.reallife: When you see a new word in science class, like 'thermometer' (therm = heat, meter = measure), roots help you guess its meaning.

items.q: Instrument for looking at faraway stars
Study of rocks and the earth

quiz.q: The root 'tele' means ___.
quiz.explain: 'Tele' means far, as in telephone (sound from far) and telescope (look far).
steps: Think of telephone (sound from far) and telescope (look far).
So 'tele' means far.
Answer: far
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'tele' with 'micro'

quiz.q: What does 'astronomy' study?
quiz.explain: 'Astro' means star, so astronomy is the study of stars and space.
steps: 'Astro' means star.
So astronomy is the study of stars and space.
Answer: Stars and space
quiz.mistake: Confuses astronomy with geology or botany

quiz.q: Which word means 'a written account of a person's life'?
quiz.explain: bio (life) + graph (write) = biography, a life story written down.
steps: bio (life) + graph (write) = biography.
A written account of a person's life.
Answer: biography
quiz.mistake: Picks 'biology', which is the study of life

quiz.q: In 'microphone', 'phone' means ___.
quiz.explain: 'Phone' means sound. A microphone picks up sound so that it can be made louder or recorded.
steps: Think of telephone and headphone — they carry sound.
So 'phone' means sound.
Answer: sound
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'phone' means a mobile phone

quiz.q: What does 'geology' mean?
options: Study of the earth and its rocks
quiz.explain: geo (earth) + logy (study of) = geology.
steps: geo (earth) + logy (study of).
Geology is the study of the earth and its rocks.
Answer: Study of the earth and its rocks
quiz.mistake: Mixes up geo with astro or bio

quiz.q: The root 'photo' in 'photosynthesis' means ___.
quiz.explain: Plants use light to make food; 'photo' means light.
steps: Plants use light to make food in photosynthesis.
So 'photo' means light.
Answer: light
quiz.mistake: Links 'photo' only with pictures

quiz.q: 'Astronaut' comes from roots meaning ___.
quiz.explain: astro (star) + naut (sailor): a 'star sailor'.
steps: astro = star, naut = sailor.
An astronaut is a 'star sailor'.
Answer: star + sailor
quiz.mistake: Does not split the word into its roots

quiz.q: Which instrument's name means 'measure heat'?
quiz.explain: therm (heat) + meter (measure) = thermometer.
steps: therm = heat, meter = measure.
So the thermometer's name means 'measure heat'.
Answer: thermometer
quiz.mistake: Picks another instrument word without checking the roots

teach.ask: Gappu sees the word 'telescope' and gets scared. How can he break it into parts to understand it?
teach.praise: Oh! Tele means far and scope means look, so a telescope helps me look at faraway things. Word roots are like secret codes!
teach.nudge: Can you split 'telescope' into two parts? What does each part mean?

revise.summary: Many science words are built from Greek or Latin roots and prefixes. Knowing the roots helps you work out what a new word means.
focus: Know the meanings of common science roots.
Split a word into roots to find its meaning.
Tell similar words apart, like biology and biography.
remember: tele = far; micro = very small; astro = star; bio = life; geo = earth; photo = light; hydro = water.
scope = look at; graph = write or draw; phone = sound; naut = sailor; logy = study of.
traps: Don't confuse 'biology' (study of life) with 'biography' (written life story).
'Phone' as a root means sound, not a mobile phone.
